issues.legal_issue: A sacred religious text installed as the central object of worship in a public place of worship may be recognized as a juristic person when the faith of its followers treats it as a living spiritual guide.
material_facts: The Guru Granth Sahib is revered by Sikhs as the continuing living Guru and the source of spiritual guidance after the line of living Gurus ended.
It is installed and worshipped as the central object in a gurdwara, where followers make obeisance and offerings to it.
The property entries at issue were made in the name of the Guru Granth Sahib installed in a dharamshala.
issues.conclusion: The Guru Granth Sahib, when installed in a gurdwara or another recognized public place of worship, is a juristic person capable of holding property; it is not equated with an idol, and every copy of the text does not thereby acquire juristic personality.
issues.legal_principle: A juristic person is an entity other than a human being to which law attributes rights and duties, and recognition may respond to the faith and needs of society. The Court relied on Pritam Dass Mahant v. Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, which recognized the Guru Granth Sahib as a juristic entity in the context of a gurdwara; Sarangadeva Periya Matam v. Ramaswami Goundar; Masjid Shahid Ganj; Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar; Som Prakash Rekhi v. Union of India; Yogendra Nath Naskar v. Commissioner of Income Tax; and Ram Jankijee Deities v. State of Bihar. The Court distinguished the recognition of the scripture from idol worship and held that installation in a public place of worship, rather than mere existence of a copy, is material.

predicates.property_rights_proceeding: A proceeding concerns whether a religious entity can hold or claim property.
predicates.scripture_installed_in_public_worship_pl: The sacred text has been installed in a public place of worship as an object of worship.
predicates.scripture_revered_as_living_spiritual_gu: Followers treat the sacred text as their continuing spiritual guide.

issues.definition: When a property-rights proceeding concerns a sacred text installed for public worship and revered as a living spiritual guide, the installed text is recognized as a juristic person.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of an appointed manager does not invalidate an endowment or negate the juristic personality of its intended recipient.
material_facts: The dispute concerned property asserted to have been dedicated for a religious and charitable purpose.
The High Court's reasoning treated the absence of a manager as a reason the religious entity could not be a juristic person.
The Supreme Court held that management could be undertaken by trustees or arranged through a court if no manager had been appointed.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a manager does not negate a juristic person's existence or cause an endowment to fail; management may be arranged through trustees or by a court in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: A juristic person need not have a manager appointed at the time of an endowment. The Court relied on Manohar Ganesh v. Lakshmiram, approved in Yogendra Nath Naskar v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and Vidyapurna Tirtha Swami v. Vidyanidhi Tirtha Swami, also approved in Yogendra Nath Naskar. It referred to the court's power under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure to make arrangements for management and to the principle that an endowment should not be allowed to fail.

rule.if: public_endowment_dispute and property_dedicated_to_public_purpose and intended_recipient_is_juristic_person and no_manager_appointed

predicates.public_endowment_dispute: A proceeding concerns property alleged to have been dedicated for a public purpose.
predicates.property_dedicated_to_public_purpose: A donor set aside property to be used for a specified public or charitable purpose.
predicates.intended_recipient_is_juristic_person: The intended recipient of the dedicated property is an entity recognized as capable of holding rights and duties.
predicates.no_manager_appointed: No manager was appointed to administer the dedicated property.

issues.definition: When property is dedicated for a public purpose to a juristic person, the lack of an appointed manager does not defeat the endowment, and management can be arranged.

issues.legal_issue: Property dedicated for public charity and entrusted to individuals only for management does not become their personal property, and their later claim to it fails where the evidence establishes the dedication and the revenue entry followed an inquiry.
material_facts: Village proprietors had given the land for the benefit of the public, including providing food and shelter to travellers, and entrusted it to the ancestors of the claimants for management.
Witnesses stated that the land was given in the name of the Guru Granth Sahib installed in the dharamshala and that the custodians had received it without payment or for services rendered.
A revenue officer held an inquiry, heard witnesses, and ordered the revenue entries changed from the custodians' names to the name of the Guru Granth Sahib installed in the dharamshala.
The custodians' ancestors did not perform the charitable duties and had sought to have the land recorded in their personal names.
The entries in the name of the religious entity remained without objection for a long period before the claimants challenged them.
The Tribunal found that the disputed property belonged to the gurdwara, and the Supreme Court upheld that result.
issues.conclusion: The property was an irrevocable public endowment, the custodians had no personal rights in it, the revenue mutations were valid, and the claim to the property was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: A public endowment, once made, is irrevocable and does not revert to the donor; persons entrusted with property for its specified purpose hold it as custodians and cannot claim it as their own. The Court held that the mutations were supported by the evidence gathered in the revenue inquiry, rather than being invalid merely because they named the Guru Granth Sahib. It also upheld the Tribunal's findings under Section 10 of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925.

rule.if: gurdwara_property_dispute and property_dedicated_for_public_charity and custodians_received_property_only_for_management and mutation_followed_evidentiary_inquiry and custodians_failed_charitable_duties and no_prior_objection_to_revenue_entry

predicates.gurdwara_property_dispute: A proceeding concerns competing claims to property associated with a gurdwara.
predicates.property_dedicated_for_public_charity: The evidence shows that the property was given for a public charitable purpose.
predicates.custodians_received_property_only_for_ma: The people who held the property received it to manage it for the designated purpose, not as personal owners.
predicates.mutation_followed_evidentiary_inquiry: A revenue authority changed the property entry after examining evidence and hearing witnesses.
predicates.custodians_failed_charitable_duties: The people entrusted with the property did not carry out the purpose for which it was entrusted.
predicates.no_prior_objection_to_revenue_entry: The earlier holders did not object to the revenue entry during the period before their later challenge.

issues.definition: Where a gurdwara-property dispute concerns a proven charitable dedication entrusted only for management, and the custodians failed their duties, an evidence-based revenue entry left unchallenged by earlier holders does not give the custodians personal title.

issues.legal_issue: A protective directive against recording dera property as a manager's personal property does not itself require entry in the name of a particular religious entity, and a mutation supported by an independent inquiry is not invalid for lacking such a direction.
material_facts: The ruler's directive stated that land belonging to a dera should not be entered as a mahant's property, but as belonging to the dera under the mahant's management.
The directive did not direct that the disputed land be entered in the name of the Guru Granth Sahib.

The revenue mutations followed applications and an inquiry in which witnesses and other evidence supported the claim that the land had been dedicated for public charity and entrusted to the custodians for management.
issues.conclusion: The directive was protective and did not itself order the disputed entries; the mutations were made on the basis of the inquiry and evidence, so they were not invalid for want of a specific direction in the directive.
issues.legal_principle: The directive required the revenue authorities to determine whether land belonged to a dera rather than personally to its mahant; it did not dictate an entry in the name of a particular religious entity. The validity of the mutations rested on the independent inquiry and evidence, not on the directive as their legal basis.

predicates.revenue_mutation_challenge: A proceeding challenges a change to an entry in the revenue records.
predicates.protective_directive_bars_personal_entry: An administrative directive prevents property belonging to a religious institution from being recorded as the personal property of its manager.
predicates.directive_does_not_name_specific_recipie: The directive does not specify the religious entity in whose name the property must be entered.
predicates.mutation_based_on_independent_evidentiar: The revenue authority changed the entry after conducting an inquiry and considering evidence independent of the directive.

issues.definition: When a protective directive bars personal recording for a manager but does not identify a specific recipient, a mutation supported by an independent evidentiary inquiry is not invalid merely because the directive did not order that entry.
